proposals.name: First disclosure versus restatement of already-public matter
proposals.instruction: Judge whether this text is putting facts into the public record for the first time. 10 = every substantive fact appears to originate here; nothing in the text signals that the events, figures or decisions were previously announced, previously covered, or already known to the reader. 5 = a mix: some genuinely new particulars wrapped around a previously announced initiative or an already-running story. 0 = the text openly presents itself as a continuation, update, reminder, or formalisation of something already announced or already reported - e.g. 'as you have likely heard by now', 'this is not a new breach', 'earlier this year we launched', 'today we are codifying the temporary policy we announced two years ago', 'the news comes after...'. Judge only the framing the text itself supplies; do not speculate about outside coverage the text does not concede.
proposals.rationale: The strongest recurring tell in the dense_low_card_high half is self-declared secondhandness. R32 (and its repeats R41, R49) opens 'As you have likely heard by now'; R47 states outright 'This theft is not a new breach, but was uncovered as part of the ongoing investigation'; R59 says the party ban was announced in August 2020 and today is merely 'codified'; R38 says the initiative was 'launched earlier this year'; R13 says 'The news comes after a collaboration agreement in Estonia last week'. Against these, R58, R28 and R21 report particulars that enter the record for the first time. A criterion bank scoring gravity, clarity, evidence and stakeholder impact has no way to see that the same material was already on the record - the item still reads as complete and important - so it over-credits every follow-up.

proposals.name: Named adversary with contested facts stated on the record
proposals.instruction: Score the presence of live, named opposition. 10 = the text identifies by name an outside party - a regulator, agency, litigant, competitor, critic, short-seller, news organisation - whose account of the facts conflicts with the issuer's, and sets out the specific points in dispute in enough detail that both accounts can be checked against each other. 5 = an outside party is named but the friction is procedural or muted, or the opponent is real but unnamed ('some have claimed'). 0 = no adversarial party appears at all; everyone mentioned is an ally, partner, customer, employee or the issuer itself.
proposals.rationale: The dense_high_card_low half is thick with named antagonism that a property-by-property bank has no slot for: R17 attacks the California DFEH by name over a three-year investigation and a pending suit; R21 names the Reno Gazette Journal, its employees, and felony assault charges; R55 rebuts an NHTSA petition it attributes to a short-seller; R11 names Expedia and Booking and their up-to-30-percent fees; R01 carries analysts and a 10 percent share fall against the company's own framing. Meanwhile the dense_low_card_high half (R08, R12, R23, R35, R39) is uniformly consensual. A bank built from 'is the claim supported', 'is the language clear', 'does it benefit stakeholders' scores a combative rebuttal no higher than a friendly programme note, because conflict is not a property of any single claim - it is a property of the configuration of parties.

proposals.name: Unhedged checkable superlative or capability claim staked publicly
proposals.instruction: Score whether the issuer stakes itself to at least one bold, unhedged, externally falsifiable assertion. 10 = a flat world- or market-scale superlative, categorical denial, or absolute capability claim that a third party could set out to disprove: 'the quickest production car in the world', 'all vehicles produced today have the hardware needed for full self-driving', 'there is no unintended acceleration in our vehicles', 'NACS vehicles outnumber CCS two-to-one'. 5 = a strong claim, but bounded or qualified into near-safety. 0 = every claim is hedged, aspirational, or unfalsifiable in principle ('we are committed to', 'we hope', 'we believe this is a step forward', 'a leader in all that we do'). Adjectival enthusiasm without a checkable referent earns nothing.
proposals.rationale: R43 and its repeat R46 lead with a ranked, benchmarked production-car claim and invite the comparison; R53 asserts that every car now leaving the factory carries full self-driving hardware; R55 issues a categorical denial that a regulator can test; R26 makes counting claims about connector share that anyone can audit. All sit in dense_high_card_low. In the other direction R08 ('achieved net-zero', 'carbon neutral cloud') and R40 ('we are committing to re-imagining this experience') read as confident and well-organised prose that a bank scoring assertiveness or ambition will credit, but neither exposes the issuer to refutation - and it is exposure, not confidence, that makes a claim worth an independent outlet's time.

proposals.name: Disclosure that cuts against the issuer's own interest
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the text works against the issuer. 10 = the item volunteers specific, particularised facts that embarrass the issuer, worsen its position, or expose it to liability - its own injury rate against an industry average, a fire in its own product, a price rise, a capability removed or software-limited, a shortfall against forecast - with figures attached. 5 = a shortcoming is acknowledged but only in generalities, or is immediately neutralised by favourable framing. 0 = every fact in the text advances the issuer's image; the item is uniformly favourable.
proposals.rationale: R57 publishes its own recordable-incident rate, concedes it is merely 'equivalent to the industry average' and 'still not where we want to be', and volunteers that two-thirds of incidents are ergonomic; R58 narrates a fire in its own vehicle in forensic detail; R24 tells buyers the price is going up, that a variant is being pulled from the ordering menu, and that its range will be limited by 10 percent with named features disabled; R01 reports a missed revenue estimate and flat profits. All are dense_high_card_low. Costly disclosure is a credibility signal a journalist weights heavily and a per-property bank cannot reward, since each individual damaging fact scores badly on any 'does this reflect well / demonstrate benefit' axis.

proposals.name: Consequences land on identified parties outside the organisation
proposals.instruction: Score who is actually changed by the action, and how wide that set is. 10 = the described action alters something concrete for people outside the issuing organisation - every customer of a product, an entire industry's equipment choices, competitors, regulators, investors - and the text makes clear who they are and roughly how many. 5 = external parties are affected but marginally, or only a small named set. 0 = nothing changes for anyone outside the organisation; the item concerns the issuer's own employees, offices, internal processes, culture or self-image only. Rhetorical invocation of 'communities' or 'the world' with no external change scores 0.
proposals.rationale: Contrast R26 (invites every charging network operator and vehicle manufacturer to adopt the connector, and publishes the files that let them) and R24 (every prospective buyer's price, ordering route and feature set changes today) with R39 (an on-site childcare centre for 116 children of the issuer's own employees at one building), R45 (internal guidelines for reopening the issuer's own offices) and R25 (the issuer's own conference moves online). The dense_low_card_high half is dominated by internally-directed acts described in the warm, stakeholder-centred language a criterion bank is built to reward; the axis it misses is simply whether anyone outside the building is affected.

proposals.name: Measurement anchored to an outside standard or published series
proposals.instruction: Score how far the item's headline numbers are anchored outside the issuer's own control. 10 = the central figures are produced under, or certified against, a named external standard, rating cycle, benchmark procedure, or a documented long-running public data series, and the text names it and points to where it can be checked. 5 = self-computed but with the methodology described well enough to be criticised. 0 = the headline number is self-defined, self-audited, or given with no methodology at all - a total 'given', a status 'achieved', a percentage with no denominator.
proposals.rationale: R34 leans on an 'official EPA-rated range of 402 miles' with the comparison vehicle named; R43 cites a named benchmark procedure for its 0-60 figure; R14, R19 and R44 are index releases whose entire content is a methodologically fixed series with 27 years of downloadable history; R57 scores itself against the published industry incident-rate average. All are dense_high_card_low, several extremely so. Against them, R08 announces net-zero with no verifying body and R30 announces a billion dollars given with no accounting at all - yet both read as substantial, quantified achievements to a bank asking 'is the claim supported by evidence in the text'. The distinction that matters to a reporter is not whether a number is present but whether someone other than the issuer stands behind it.

proposals.name: Mechanism-level detail only the issuer could supply
proposals.instruction: Score the presence of insider detail about how, not just what. 10 = the text explains how the thing works or how the change was achieved at a level no outsider could reconstruct - component counts, coefficients, before-and-after parameter values, architecture, failure paths, unit economics. 5 = some specifics, but of a kind an outsider could infer or look up. 0 = outcomes, adjectives and intentions only; nothing a reader could reason with, check, or build on.
proposals.rationale: R16 gives cell energy up 31 percent, drag coefficient 0.36 to 0.31, rolling resistance 11.0 to 8.9 kg/ton; R53 gives eight cameras, twelve ultrasonic sensors, forty-times compute, and names the redundancy argument; R58 gives a 25-ton peak force, a 16-module pack, and the exact vent path the flames took plus what the fire crew did wrong; R34 itemises the mass, wheel, drive-unit and regeneration changes behind a range figure. All dense_high_card_low. In the other direction R23, R35 and R60 describe programmes with no mechanism at all. Mechanism is what makes an item reportable without a follow-up call, and it is invisible to criteria phrased as 'is the announcement specific' - the promotional items are specific too, just not about mechanism.

proposals.name: Complete self-contained text a reporter could file from
proposals.instruction: Score whether the supplied text is by itself a whole item. 10 = subject, action, particulars and enough context to write from are all present in the text; nothing essential is deferred to a linked video, gallery, report, chart page or dataset. 5 = substantive but visibly truncated, or with one important element deferred. 0 = the text is a teaser, a caption, a headline plus 'take a look', a page of navigation furniture, or an extraction artefact containing no release at all. Judge only the completeness of the text in front of you, never the importance of the topic it gestures at.
proposals.rationale: This is the sharpest single failure visible in the slice. R31 contains no press release whatsoever - only a note that the page held no identifiable body text - and yet sits in the dense_low_card_high half, meaning the scorecard rated an empty shell highly. R30 is a two-sentence headline followed by 'Take a look:'; R22 defers its evidence to 'the video below' and 'the gallery below'; R60 defers to 'the pages of this report'. A bank of criteria each scored 0-10 by a judge will hand out mid-range partial credit on tone, topic and apparent seriousness even when there is nothing to score, and those partial credits aggregate into a high total. A single explicit substance-present gate catches all four.

proposals.name: Discrete dated event versus programme, principle or intention
proposals.instruction: Score whether something actually happened. 10 = a specific act, completed or taking effect on a stated date, performed by identified actors - a document filed, a price changed, a suit met, an incident occurred, a figure published, a standard released. 5 = a real event exists but is buried in process and philosophy, or is scheduled without mechanism. 0 = the text describes an approach, a set of guiding principles, a way of thinking, an internal Q&A about how decisions get made, or an intention to consider something later; nothing in it can be given a date.
proposals.rationale: R45 offers 'guiding principles we are thinking about', a 'Guideline Matrix', and a return 'when the time is right'; R40 commits to 're-imagining this experience' and to coming out of a conference with 'an actionable plan'; R06 is two executives answering questions about how remodels are approached. All three are dense_low_card_high and all three are long, earnest, well-structured and full of the stakeholder language a bank rewards. Against them R28 ('today confidentially submitted' a specific form to a specific regulator), R24 ('beginning today', with prices and effective changes) and R21 (a dated incident with times, injuries and charges) are events. Eventfulness is the oldest news criterion there is and is the easiest thing for a property-based scorecard to miss, because process prose scores well on every property taken one at a time.

proposals.name: Primary-source artifact released with the announcement
proposals.instruction: Score whether the item hands over primary material rather than only summarising it. 10 = the text reproduces or releases something a reporter can quote and inspect directly - a verbatim internal email or letter, reproduced correspondence with a named third party, downloadable specification or design files, the full underlying data series, a filed document. 5 = extensive verbatim quotation from a single named principal, but no artifact. 0 = nothing but the issuer's own summarising prose, optionally with a marketing link.
proposals.rationale: R02 and its repeat R37 are the internal email itself, reproduced verbatim including its asides; R58 reprints the vehicle owner's own correspondence with permission; R26 makes the design and specification files available for download and says so; R14, R19 and R44 point to the whole underlying series. All are dense_high_card_low, several at the top of the slice. An artifact converts a release from a claim into evidence, which is precisely what determines whether an independent outlet can write from it without depending on the issuer; a criterion bank scoring the prose has no reason to notice that the prose is not the payload.

proposals.name: General-public stake versus narrow professional-specialty relevance
proposals.instruction: Score the breadth of the constituency with a stake in the subject. 10 = the subject bears on something any general reader belongs to or immediately recognises - house prices, car prices, a mass-market product's fortunes, personal payment data, a household-name company's results. 5 = a large but bounded professional or regional audience. 0 = the material is legible and useful only inside one professional specialty - monthly import tonnages by product grade, a fleet-age statistic framed toward aftermarket repair revenue, origination-fee accounting for one lending programme, the briefing schedule in one regulatory suit. Score the audience for the subject matter, explicitly not the quality of the writing or the density of the numbers.
proposals.rationale: R03 (crude and fuel-oil tonnages month over month), R04 (average fleet age, framed toward aftermarket repair revenue), R07 (PPP origination fees across community banks), R52 (Nigerian downstream price-cap removal) and R54 (proposed cross-motion dates in a mine-safety rule challenge) are all dense_low_card_high, and all of them are quantitative, sourced, coherent and expert - exactly the profile a criterion bank rewards. R14 and R01 are just as quantitative but concern house prices and a phone everyone owns. The variable separating the two groups is who the numbers are for, and it is orthogonal to every text-quality property a bank is likely to contain.

proposals.name: First-party announcement versus third-party recap of others
proposals.instruction: Score who is speaking and about whom. 10 = the issuing organisation is announcing its own action, in its own name, on the record, and is accountable for every claim made. 5 = an issuer release built substantially out of other parties' previously published statements or data. 0 = the text is a finished news article, analyst note or trade write-up about other organisations' activity - reporter framing, a byline or dateline in outlet style, quotes gathered from several outside spokesmen, no announcement by anyone. Judge the speaking position, not the topic.
proposals.rationale: R51 is an aviation trade outlet's write-up of an airport lapse, quoting a border-agency representative, an airport representative and an airline representative in turn; R52, R54, R07 and R03 are likewise outlet copy about third parties, complete with 'Singapore --' and 'London --' datelines and analyst sourcing. All are dense_low_card_high. Nobody in them is announcing anything, so there is no organisation putting its name behind a new fact - which is what an independent outlet would be picking up. A criterion bank evaluating sourcing, balance and evidentiary support will actively prefer this material, because finished journalism scores well on exactly those axes; the speaking position is the one thing it cannot see.

proposals.name: Counter-expectation: act violates the normal script for such an organisation
proposals.instruction: Score how far the described act departs from what an organisation of this type would ordinarily be expected to do. 10 = the act cuts against the organisation's obvious self-interest or its standing posture - giving away a proprietary standard to competitors, co-operating operationally with its closest rival, publicly attacking the regulator that oversees it, courting the customers of the incumbents it is displacing by open letter. 5 = mildly unusual, or a familiar act performed at unusual scale. 0 = precisely what such an organisation routinely does: a seasonal sale, a benefits expansion, a sustainability report, a partnership with an obvious ally, a charitable milestone. Judge the departure from the expected script, not the size of the action.
proposals.rationale: R26 opens a proprietary connector design to the whole industry and publishes the files; R48 has two directly competing platforms building a shared removals list through a trusted intermediary; R11 is an open letter courting the boutique operators of the incumbent booking agencies while naming their fee levels; R10 has an actor and ceramicist personally hosting overnight guests in his own studio. All four sit in dense_high_card_low with wide gaps. Surprise is relational - it lives in the mismatch between actor and act - so it cannot be scored by any single-property criterion about clarity, evidence, specificity or benefit, each of which these items would pass or fail on grounds unrelated to why they are interesting.

proposals.name: Firm imminent public date versus indefinite timing
proposals.instruction: Score the precision of the timing the item commits to. 10 = the text fixes an exact date, and usually a time, at which something the audience is waiting for happens or becomes available, and spells out the mechanics of taking part - an unveiling, a reservation opening, a booking window, a shareholder meeting with a registration deadline. 5 = a date exists but attaches to something routine, or a window is given without mechanics. 0 = timing is indefinite or absent - 'in the coming months', 'later this year', 'when the time is right', 'dates, cities and details to follow'.
proposals.rationale: R20 fixes reservations worldwide on March 31, an unveil at 8:30pm PT, and per-region queue mechanics; R05 fixes 1:30 PM Pacific on September 22 with a second event immediately after, plus a password, a control-number route and a 2:00 PM deadline; R10 opens booking February 7 at 10:00 AM PT for three named nights at a stated price; R28 pins its offering to the completion of a specified regulatory review. All dense_high_card_low, including two items whose underlying substance is thin. Against them R45 returns 'when the time is right', R48 launches 'in the coming months', R40 promises 'dates, cities and details to follow'. A hard date is a peg an outlet can schedule against; vague futurity is the standard tell of an announcement with nothing behind it, and neither is a property of the claims a bank scores.

proposals.name: Promotional selling register versus neutral declarative register
proposals.instruction: Score the register of the text independently of how specific its facts are. 10 = it reports - declarative third person or plain first person, no exhortation, no exclamation, no offers, no second-person shopping instruction, no calls to action. 5 = informative but with promotional passages or a closing pitch. 0 = it is advertising: discounts and prices are the payload, the reader is addressed as a shopper and told what to do ('get excited', 'you won't want to miss', 'be sure to check your local store', 'limit two per guest'), and the mechanics of purchase are the substance of the item.
proposals.rationale: R50 is 'Save $20 for every $100 you spend' with a stacking rule; R22 is 'get ready', 'oh-so much more to love', prices from $1.25 to $49.99, and a gallery of partner brands; R33 is 'Hoping to get your hands on one? Here are a few tips', with a price, a per-guest limit and store timing; R06 is 'get excited!' plus an interview about store aesthetics. All four are dense_low_card_high, and all four are concrete, well-organised, dated, priced and clearly beneficial to the reader - which is to say they will score well on nearly every property a criterion bank is likely to contain, including specificity, clarity and stakeholder benefit. What disqualifies them is not any missing property but the purpose the whole text serves, which needs its own axis to be visible at all.

proposals.name: Character-encoding damage and text-extraction residue
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the passage carries character-encoding damage and page-extraction residue. Count visible artefacts such as: apostrophes or accents collapsed into stray letters (for example 'weare' where 'we're' was meant, 'Iam' for 'I'm', 'worldas' for 'world's', 'aa' or 'a' standing in for a dash or curly quote); isolated stray capital letters wedged mid-sentence or in runs; whole blocks of identical text repeated back-to-back; leftover navigation, category chrome, code fences, stray braces or quotation marks; commentary about the page rather than content of the page. 0 = clean, well-formed prose with no such artefacts anywhere. 5 = artefacts appear in a noticeable minority of sentences. 10 = artefacts are pervasive, affecting most sentences or leaving the text partly unreadable. Score ONLY how much artefact material is visible. You must NOT judge whether the text is well written, clear, professional, interesting or important, and you must not let the subject matter or the identity of the organisation move the score.
proposals.rationale: MODE 1 surface. R07, R22, R26 and R59 are shot through with the same mangled-apostrophe pattern ('Iam', 'weare', 'worldas', 'itas', stray 'A' runs), and R53 consists of nothing but a stray closing brace, a code fence and a scraper's own note about the page. The damage is concentrated in the pages of one publisher, so it tags a whole block of items with a signature that a text-only model can read as a feature. Nothing about a mangled apostrophe bears on whether a journalist would write the release up; the parent is purely an ingestion pipeline, so this is a clean nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: the publisher's content-management system and the page-scraping/text-extraction path used to ingest that publisher's pages

proposals.name: Fragment cut off mid-sentence versus complete document
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the passage is a fragment that has been cut off rather than a complete document. Evidence for a high score: the text stops mid-sentence, mid-clause or mid-word; there is no concluding sentence, sign-off, contact block or closing paragraph; a section or list is announced and then not delivered; the final line trails into nothing. Evidence for a low score: the text ends on a fully formed final sentence, a sign-off, a boilerplate closer or an evident conclusion. 0 = clearly complete and closed. 10 = breaks off in the middle of a word or clause with an obviously unfinished final section. Score ONLY the completeness of the span in front of you. You must NOT judge whether the content is substantive, good, thorough or important, and you must not infer anything about quality from the fact that a document is long enough to have been cut.
proposals.rationale: MODE 1 surface. R03, R23, R27, R37, R46 and R52 all break off in mid-sentence, while R29, R42 and R49 close cleanly. Truncation here is an artefact of a length cap applied at ingestion and is mechanically determined by the original document's length, so a model can learn 'ends mid-word' as a usable signal. No journalist reading the real release ever sees the cut, so the trace can only be a nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: the fixed text-length cap applied when the corpus was assembled, which is itself downstream of how long the original document was

proposals.name: Consumer purchase-mechanics and promotional offer density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the text is built around consumer-facing purchase mechanics. Count: named shelf or booking prices a shopper would pay; percentage-off, spend-and-save or dollar-off offer structures; promotional windows and shop-by or on-sale dates; gift-card, coupon, cleanse-price, limit-per-customer or cannot-be-combined terms; availability and where-to-look tips; second-person urging to shop, book, check a store or hurry; exclamation-marked enthusiasm about a deal. 0 = no purchase-mechanics material at all. 5 = a section of the text is offer mechanics, the rest is not. 10 = the text is essentially a shopping offer from start to finish. Score ONLY how much of this material is present. You must NOT judge whether the offer is attractive, well written, generous or worthwhile.
proposals.rationale: MODE 1 surface, with an honest upstream parent. R06 is a spend-and-save offer with two dated windows and a combination restriction; R33 is a stock-availability tip sheet with a $59.99 price, a two-per-guest limit and dated drops; R36 lists price bands from $1.25 to $49.99 plus product counts; R52 sets a $421 rate and a 10:00 AM PT booking time; R01 wraps a giving milestone in the same shop-friendly voice. Offer-mechanics density identifies the desk that produced the item, which is exactly the sort of provenance a text model can latch onto. Tagged mixed because the producing desk plausibly also bears on genuine news value, so this must appear in the sensitivity band rather than being discounted outright.
proposals.upstream_parent: which internal function produced the item (a merchandising/consumer-marketing desk versus a corporate communications, policy or investor-relations desk)

proposals.name: Named-individual personal-voice signature on the document
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the text is voiced as a personal communication from a named individual rather than as an impersonal organisational statement. Count: first-person-singular pronouns ('I', 'me', 'my'); a salutation opening ('Dear ...'); autobiographical framing of the writer's own tenure, role, career length or feelings; an explicit frame stating that the passage is an email, letter or message from a named person; a closing signature giving a personal name, often with a job title; direct expressions of personal thanks, apology or pride in the first person singular. 0 = no personal-voice markers anywhere; the text speaks only as an organisation or in the third person. 10 = the entire text is a signed first-person letter or message. Score ONLY how much personal-voice marking is visible. You must NOT judge whether the personal voice is sincere, appropriate, effective or well executed, and you must not treat a senior-sounding title as evidence of anything.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 upstream-factor. The unseen factor is authorship and seniority; its textual fingerprint is the signature apparatus. R03 opens 'Dear Host' and is explicitly framed as an email from a named co-founder; R08 is a first-person account by a newly hired safety head ('When I recently joined Tesla'); R10 closes with a named chairman and CEO; R16, R44 and R58 are signed guest letters; R27 signs off '-- Elon'; R30 and R47 are framed as an email just sent to employees. The judge scores only the visible signature apparatus, never the unobservable seniority. Tagged mixed because a personally signed item may genuinely mark an occasion the organisation considers weighty.
proposals.upstream_parent: who inside the organisation drafted and put their name to the item (a named senior executive writing personally versus an unnamed communications team)

proposals.name: Defensive posture toward a named external actor or incident
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the text is written against a specific named external actor or a specific external incident, rather than presenting an initiative of the organisation's own choosing. Count: naming of a regulator, government agency, court, prosecutor, law firm, news outlet, reporter, critic, investor or petitioner and then disputing, rebutting, correcting, blaming or apologising to them; rebuttal and denial syntax ('this is completely false', 'it strains credibility', 'contrary to reports', 'we deeply regret', 'we are truly sorry', 'this is both unfair'); narration of an accident, breach, arrest, lawsuit, investigation, complaint or failure that originated outside the organisation and to which the text is reacting; forensic detail supplied to counter an outside account. 0 = wholly self-initiated framing with no external challenger or incident named. 10 = the text exists entirely as a response to a named outside challenge. Score ONLY how much of this reactive material is present. You must NOT judge whether the response is convincing, justified, well handled or fair.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 upstream-factor. The unseen factor is the trigger for issuing at all; the fingerprint is the rebuttal apparatus. R20 attacks a named state agency at length; R25 narrates an incident with named newspaper employees and a sheriff's department; R49 opens by calling a petition false and attributing it to a short-seller; R27 reconstructs a vehicle fire against an outside account; R31 narrates a failed settlement in litigation; R11 discloses further breach findings. A judge can score the visible defensiveness without knowing what actually forced the release. Tagged mixed honestly: crises are both a nuisance parent and, often, genuinely consequential.
proposals.upstream_parent: whether an external event, adversary or regulatory action forced the communication (crisis-response trigger) rather than the organisation choosing its own moment

proposals.name: Direct servicing of a named non-press stakeholder audience
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the text addresses and operationally services an existing named audience -- customers, hosts, employees, members, owners, shareholders -- rather than a general reader. Count: a salutation naming that audience; sustained second-person 'you/your' directed at them; step-by-step procedures they must follow; eligibility rules, cut-offs, deadlines and enrolment or registration mechanics; dedicated URLs, hotlines, email addresses, passwords, control numbers or reference codes they are told to use; reassurance or instruction framed around what they personally should do next; house-internal membership vocabulary used without explanation as if the reader is already inside. 0 = none of this; the text is written outward to a general reader. 10 = the text is essentially an operating-instruction sheet for a specific existing audience. Score ONLY how much servicing material is present. You must NOT judge whether the instructions are helpful, generous, clear or well designed.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 upstream-factor. The unseen factor is who the document was actually written to reach; the fingerprint is the servicing apparatus. R16, R44 and R58 open 'Dear Target Guest' and hand the reader enrolment steps and monitoring advice; R03 routes hosts to airbnb.com/250msupport and airbnb.com/superhostrelief; R40 addresses boutique-hotel and B&B owners and closes with an email address; R56 supplies a meeting password, a fifteen-digit control-number procedure and dated deadlines. Servicing density measures the document's operational purpose, which is a different thing from whether an outside newsroom would run it, so the parent is treated as pure nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: the document's intended primary recipient and delivery channel (an operational message to an existing stakeholder list, later posted publicly, versus an item written for outside readers)

proposals.name: Outside-reporter authorship fingerprint rather than organisational voice
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the passage reads as written ABOUT organisations by an outside reporter or analyst, rather than BY the organisation it concerns. Count: consistent third-person reference to every company and agency involved, with no first-person 'we/our' organisational voice anywhere; attribution formulas ('according to', 'analysts say', 'data released on Tuesday showed', 'told the court', 'a representative commented'); quotations from outside experts, officials, rival parties or named individuals at other organisations; a personal reporter or analyst byline, a wire-style city dateline, a photo credit, a subscription or alerts interruption; a headline that summarises a development in the world rather than announcing the organisation's own action; even-handed presentation of two or more sides. 0 = a pure first-person organisational statement. 10 = pure outside-reporter or analyst copy with no organisational voice at all. Score ONLY the authorial stance visible in the text. You must NOT judge whether the reporting is accurate, interesting, well sourced or important.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 upstream-factor. The unseen factor is corpus provenance; the fingerprint is authorial stance. R19 and R54 carry Platts-style single-city datelines, customs and regulator data and no first-person voice; R23 and R46 quote named analysts and executives at other firms in third person; R31 narrates a court docket from outside; R35 quotes a border agency, an airport and an airline in turn; R50 is a newspaper market report complete with a photograph credit and an after-hours share move. Compare R02, R38 and R29, which are first-person organisational statements throughout. Provenance sorts the slice into two populations for reasons entirely separate from merit. Tagged mixed because an item that already exists as journalism is not independent of what journalists find worth writing.
proposals.upstream_parent: how the item entered the corpus -- whether the organisation authored and issued it at all, or whether a third-party trade-press or newspaper article was collected alongside genuine releases

proposals.name: Presupposition of earlier instalments in the same programme
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the text assumes the reader already knows earlier instalments of the same programme, policy or data series, rather than introducing its subject from scratch. Count: explicit back-references ('as we announced in August 2020', 'earlier this year we launched', 'this follows', 'the news comes after', 'since 2016 we have', 'building on', 'an update to', 'the latest results'); recaps of prior steps presented as shared background; ordinal, cumulative or streak framing ('the fifth straight year', 'more than 27 years of history', 'the third quarter in a row', 'another milestone'); statements that the item is a routine periodic or scheduled release; references to a named prior initiative, policy or announcement without explaining it. Score low where the subject, programme or product is introduced cold, defined on first mention, and framed as new or first-of-its-kind. 0 = fully self-contained, introduces everything from scratch. 10 = unreadable without prior instalments and explicitly framed as the next one in a run. Score ONLY the amount of presupposition and back-reference visible. You must NOT judge whether continuity is good practice, whether the programme is worthwhile, or whether the update matters.
proposals.rationale: MODE 3 position-in-container. The unseen factor is ordinal position in the release stream; the fingerprint is presupposition load. R02 stacks back-references ('The news comes after', 'Earlier last month', 'Since 2016, Airbnb has reported in Ireland'); R21 opens on 'Earlier this year, we launched our Live and Work Anywhere initiative'; R38 recaps 'In August 2020 we announced a temporary ban' and narrates 'How we got here'; R09, R39 and R43 are explicitly the latest instalment of a monthly series with 'more than 27 years of history'; R11 states the theft 'is not a new breach' but an extension of a previously disclosed one; R23 notes 'the fifth straight year'. Against these, R24 and R29 introduce their subject cold. Tagged mixed because being first-of-its-kind in a series may itself carry genuine news value.
proposals.upstream_parent: position of the item in the organisation's own run of releases on that programme (a first-of-its-kind announcement versus the twentieth routine update in an established series)

proposals.name: Anchoring to a calendar, fiscal or news-cycle moment
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the text anchors itself to a specific point in the commercial, fiscal or news calendar. Count: named holidays, shopping days and seasonal moments ('Green Monday, Dec. 11', 'with just a few weeks left until Christmas', 'Happy Holidays', 'this holiday season', 'to start the year'); fiscal-period framing ('the final few weeks of this quarter', 'fourth quarter', 'year-over-year', 'annual meeting', 'looking back on 2015'); periodic data-cadence framing ('data released today for September 2022', 'preliminary data released on Tuesday', monthly or quarterly series language); conference, event or tour season framing; explicit day-level or hour-level scheduling of when something opens, launches, ships or when the reader must act; a prominent standalone date line or day-of-week marker. 0 = no calendar anchoring at all; the text would read identically in any week of any year. 10 = the text is organised end to end around a calendar moment. Score ONLY the amount of calendar anchoring visible. You must NOT judge whether the timing is apt, clever or significant, and you must not reason about whether the date was a busy or quiet news day.
proposals.rationale: MODE 3 position-in-container, calendar arm, with a MODE 4 timing-convention component. The unseen factor is when the item was pushed out; the fingerprint is date and season language. R06 is built entirely on 'Green Monday, Dec. 11' with a dated toy window; R33 counts down 'a few weeks left until Christmas' with drops on Dec. 11; R41 closes 'Happy Holidays' and promises a demonstration 'in the early weeks of 2015'; R30 and R47 open on 'the final few weeks of this quarter'; R09, R39 and R43 are month-stamped instalments of a fixed monthly data cadence; R56 is pinned to a dated annual meeting with hour-level deadlines; R01 carries a bare 'August 31, 2015'. Calendar position is upstream of both issuance and how crowded the receiving day is, and the trace is fully visible in the text. Tagged mixed because quarter-end and earnings-cadence items can carry real substance.
proposals.upstream_parent: timing of issuance within the calendar and the news cycle (quarter-end, earnings and index-release cadence, shopping and holiday season, conference season, scheduled-event conventions)

proposals.name: Paid-newswire and formal-distribution furniture versus house-blog chrome
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the item is wrapped in the furniture of formal or paid-newswire distribution. Count toward a HIGH score: an all-caps or city-plus-date dateline heading the item ('MINNEAPOLIS - July 7, 2014', 'NEW YORK, NOVEMBER 29, 2022:', 'TEANECK, N.J. and LONDON'); a wire-service credit line; stock ticker and exchange in parentheses after a company name; a standing 'About [Company]' boilerplate paragraph; securities-law, Rule 135 or forward-looking-statement disclaimers and formal third-person self-reference ('the Company'); media-contact blocks, 'sign up to receive updates' lines, standardised URL or registration footers; a subheading written as a formal benefit statement. Count toward a LOW score: house-blog chrome such as a byline reading 'By [Company]' followed by a date and topic tags, a collective team signature, duplicated 'Key Takeaways' blocks, conversational headings, or no masthead furniture at all. 0 = no formal-distribution furniture whatsoever. 10 = formal furniture surrounds the item end to end. Score ONLY the visible furniture. You must NOT judge whether formal distribution is more professional, more credible, or whether the announcement is important.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4 corpus upstream priors. The unseen factors are who drafted the item and what channel it went out on; the fingerprint is masthead and boilerplate furniture. R55 carries a wire credit line, an all-caps two-city dateline, exchange tickers for both parties, a formal benefit subheading and an 'About Cognizant' block; R48 carries a MINNEAPOLIS dateline, '(NYSE: TGT)' and an 'About Target' block; R24 is almost pure Rule 135 securities boilerplate; R09, R39 and R43 open on an all-caps NEW YORK dateline with a 'Sign up to receive updates' line. Against these, R02 and R28 carry blog chrome ('By Airbnb * date, Policy') and duplicated Key Takeaways blocks, and R04, R17 and R29 carry only a collective team signature. The trace separates distribution tier and drafting desk, which is not the same thing as news value. Tagged mixed because an organisation's choice to pay for wire distribution may itself track how consequential it believes the item to be.
proposals.upstream_parent: distribution tier and drafting function (an outside PR agency or investor-relations/legal desk pushing to a paid newswire versus an in-house communications team posting to the organisation's own newsroom CMS)

proposals.name: Numeric claim anchored to a named comparison benchmark
proposals.instruction: Score how precisely the release grounds its central claim in verifiable numbers explicitly compared against a named external benchmark (a competitor product, a prior year's own figure, an industry record, or a third-party index reading). A 10: the release states a specific quantitative result (e.g., a percentage, time, distance, price) and explicitly compares it to one or more named external reference points, making the claim checkable by an outside reader. A 0: the release uses only vague evaluative language ('leading,' 'significant,' 'best-in-class') with no number, or gives numbers with no named point of comparison.
proposals.rationale: R05 states a precise 402-mile EPA range and compares it explicitly to the 2019 Model S 100D's rating; R07/R28 state a 2.5-second 0-60 time and name the LaFerrari and Porsche 918 Spyder as the comparison set. Contrast R01, which describes a 'mobile money opportunity' and 'topline growth' with no checkable number or named comparator at all.

proposals.name: Forensic minute-by-minute reconstruction of a specific incident
proposals.instruction: Score how much the release reads as a minute-by-minute forensic reconstruction of a single real-world incident, with times, sequence of actions, and measurable outcomes (injuries, damage, dimensions). A 10: the text gives a clear timeline of what happened, in order, with concrete measurable detail (a time of day, a size of injury or damage, a specific force or distance). A 0: the release contains no incident narrative at all, only general statements or policy language.
proposals.rationale: R02 gives a minute-level account ('approximately 11:50 am') with specific injuries (a '2" bleeding laceration'); R08 reconstructs the sequence of the road-debris strike and fire with a measured '3 inch diameter hole' and '25 tons' of force. Compare R11 or R34, which contain no incident at all, only retrospective summary language.

proposals.name: Explicit rebuttal of a named external accuser
proposals.instruction: Score how directly the release names and factually rebuts an external accusation, lawsuit, petition, or critical claim made by an identified outside party. A 10: the release names the specific accuser/petitioner/agency and the specific allegation, then offers a point-by-point factual counter. A 0: the release contains no external accusation or criticism to respond to.
proposals.rationale: R45 names the short-seller petition to NHTSA and rebuts the 'unintended acceleration' allegation point by point; R57 names the California DFEH, describes the alleged lawsuit, and rebuts it with the agency's own investigation history. Compare R47 or R31, which contain no accusation to rebut.

proposals.name: Physical safety, injury, or crime stakes
proposals.instruction: Score the degree to which the release describes actual or statistically quantified risk of physical injury, death, or violent/criminal conduct. A 10: the release describes an actual injury, death, assault, fire, or crime, or cites a specific injury/fatality statistic. A 0: the release contains no physical-safety content of any kind.
proposals.rationale: R02 describes a felony assault causing bleeding lacerations; R60 cites NHTSA's estimate that 'over 900 people were killed' by backing vehicles; R08 describes a battery fire. Compare R25 (a toy discount) or R11 (a CSR letter), which carry zero physical-safety content.

proposals.name: Superlative claim anchored to named comparators
proposals.instruction: Score whether a 'first,' 'fastest,' 'largest,' or similar superlative claim is anchored to an explicitly named set of comparators that a reader could independently check. A 10: the superlative names the specific competing products/companies/records it is being measured against. A 0: the release uses superlative language ('leading,' 'best,' 'the way we do it best') with no named comparator at all.
proposals.rationale: R07/R28 claim third-fastest-ever acceleration and explicitly name the LaFerrari and Porsche 918 Spyder as the only faster cars; R22 claims full self-driving hardware at a safety level 'substantially greater than that of a human driver.' Contrast R42, whose claim (Mexico City becoming a 'global hub' for remote workers) names no comparator set at all.

proposals.name: Concrete, dated, immediately-available deliverable
proposals.instruction: Score whether the release describes a specific action, product, or policy change with a stated date that is now (or imminently) available or in effect, versus describing only an intention, partnership, or alliance with no concrete deliverable. A 10: a specific, dated change that a customer/reader can act on or observe starting now or on a stated near-term date. A 0: only an abstract statement of intent, collaboration, or aspiration with no concrete, dated deliverable.
proposals.rationale: R22 states that, 'as of today,' all Tesla vehicles being produced now have new hardware; R31 states Superchargers are launching now in 'downtown Chicago and Boston.' Compare R01 (a Cognizant/Monitise 'alliance' with no product, date, or deliverable named) and R42, which describes only future 'trainings' and partnerships with no concrete date.

proposals.name: Density of vague corporate B2B jargon
proposals.instruction: Score the density of vague, evaluative corporate jargon phrases ('capitalize on the opportunity,' 'drive topline growth,' 'reshape the channel mix,' 'unlock synergies') relative to concrete informational content. A 10: nearly every sentence uses such jargon in place of concrete facts. A 0: the text is plainly factual with no jargon padding.
proposals.rationale: R01 is saturated with phrases like 'capitalize on the mobile money opportunity,' 'drive newer revenue streams,' and 'redraws the ways in which businesses engage with customers,' with almost no concrete fact underneath. Compare R16, a Case-Shiller data release, which is plain factual reporting with essentially no jargon.

proposals.name: Breadth of directly affected general public
proposals.instruction: Score how broad and general the population directly affected by the release's subject matter is, versus how narrow/specialized the affected audience is. A 10: the subject (e.g., a national home-price index, a mass data breach) directly touches the finances or safety of a very large, general population (homeowners, consumers nationwide). A 0: the subject matters only to a narrow professional/trade audience (e.g., commodity traders, a single regulatory docket) and has no direct bearing on the general public.
proposals.rationale: R16 and R54 report the S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller national home-price index, which bears directly on the finances of most American homeowners and renters. Compare R53 (China's monthly crude oil import volumes) and R23 (average US vehicle age from S&P Global Mobility), which are narrow trade/industry statistics with no direct bearing on a general reader's own finances or safety.

proposals.name: Self-congratulatory internal milestone framing
proposals.instruction: Score how much the release frames a voluntary, self-initiated achievement in self-congratulatory 'milestone' or 'proud' language, celebrating the organization's own values or generosity, without any external party (regulator, critic, reporter) having prompted or scrutinized the action. A 10: heavy self-congratulatory language ('we're proud,' 'we did it,' 'milestone') describing a purely voluntary internal accomplishment. A 0: no self-congratulatory framing; the release is a plain statement of fact or is a response to an external party.
proposals.rationale: R34 ('We Did it! Target Gives $1 Billion for Education') and R52 ('we're thrilled to announce the grand opening' of a new childcare center) both frame purely voluntary, self-initiated actions in celebratory language with no external prompt. Compare R57, which responds to an actual outside lawsuit rather than celebrating an internal achievement.

proposals.name: Externally imposed trigger for the release
proposals.instruction: Score how clearly the release's occasion is an external requirement, investigation, lawsuit, new law, or public controversy, as opposed to being timed purely at the organization's own discretion for promotional purposes. A 10: the text itself states the release is required or prompted by an external law, regulator, investigation, or public controversy. A 0: nothing in the text suggests any external prompt; the timing appears to be purely the organization's own promotional choice.
proposals.rationale: R13 (Airbnb host tax reporting) is explicitly triggered by 'changes to the law that require platforms to share host booking details'; R47 (Airbnb's confidential S-1 filing) is explicitly filed 'pursuant to... Rule 135' of the Securities Act. Compare R25 (a discretionary Green Monday sale) or R03 (a discretionary Airbnb/Houseplant promotion), which are timed purely for the organization's own promotional purposes.

proposals.name: Individually named, unscripted personal voice
proposals.instruction: Score whether the release includes a specific named individual (other than a titled executive delivering boilerplate remarks) speaking or acting in their own voice about a specific, non-generic situation -- for example a reprinted personal email, a named eyewitness, or a named ordinary employee/customer describing a specific event. A 10: a specific named non-spokesperson individual's own words or actions are quoted/described in a specific situation. A 0: only generic corporate collective voice ('our guests,' 'our team,' 'we') or scripted executive-quote boilerplate appears.
proposals.rationale: R08 reprints an actual email exchange with a named customer, 'robert Carlson,' describing his personal experience; R02 identifies specific named departments and individuals (Tesla safety managers, Sheriff's deputies) acting in a real unscripted sequence. Compare R11 and R25, which speak only in generic collective 'we'/'guests' language.

proposals.name: Garbled, corrupted, or non-substantive text
proposals.instruction: Score the coherence and integrity of the text as genuine, readable press-release/article prose. A 10: fully coherent, properly punctuated, on-topic prose throughout. A 0: the text is garbled by encoding corruption (systematically mangled apostrophes/quotation marks, broken characters) or is not actually press-release content at all (e.g., a scraper/model error message, a truncated or off-topic fragment).
proposals.rationale: R35 is not press-release content at all -- it is a scraper/model error message stating 'The provided raw page content does not appear to contain a press release'; R12 shows systematic encoding corruption with apostrophes rendered as stray 'a' characters ('Iam helping develop Salesforceas plan'), and the same corruption pattern recurs across R36, R38, and R41.

proposals.name: Stated population or dollar scale at risk
proposals.instruction: Score whether the release states a specific number of people affected or a specific dollar amount at stake, tied to a concrete risk, harm, or commitment to those people. A 10: a specific, large population count or dollar figure is given and tied to a stated risk or benefit to that population (e.g., 'up to 70 million individuals,' 'we will pay $250 million to hosts'). A 0: no such population-or-dollar-scale figure tied to a concrete risk/benefit is given.
proposals.rationale: R40 states the breach affected 'up to 70 million individuals'; R09/R32/R55 (the Target breach letter) describe unauthorized access to payment-card data for guests during a specific date window. Compare R06 (a list of 20 destinations with no affected-population figure) or R42, which give no comparable scale figure tied to concrete risk or benefit.

proposals.name: Consumer sales-copy promotional register
proposals.instruction: Score how much the release reads like consumer marketing/advertising copy -- exclamation points, playful or urgent calls to action, appeals to desire or fear-of-missing-out -- rather than informational reporting. A 10: heavy sales-copy voice (exclamation points, urgency language, playful slang, direct appeals to 'shop now'/'book now'/'don't miss out'). A 0: plain, neutral, informational register throughout with no sales-copy markers.
proposals.rationale: R03 ('Gloopy groupies and people who like nice things residing in the U.S. can request to book...') and R17 ('Hatchimal Hunt Have You Scrambled? Keep Your Eyes on Target Next Week') are both written in a playful, urgency-driven consumer marketing voice. Compare R16 or R51, which stay in a neutral, informational register even where R51 concerns Apple's own commercial results.

proposals.name: Internal operational detail without external consequence
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the release consists of specific-sounding operational/administrative numbers (headcounts, capacities, counts of internal items) describing a matter whose consequence is confined to the organization's own internal operations, with no described effect on outside parties or the public. A 10: the release is dense with precise internal operational figures (e.g., number of classrooms, number of ideas submitted, number of office locations) but the underlying matter has no stated effect beyond the organization itself. A 0: the release contains no such internal-operations figures, or any such figures are directly tied to an external consequence.
proposals.rationale: R41 cites 'more than 65,000 ideas' submitted to Salesforce's internal IdeaExchange product-feedback tool, with no stated effect on outside parties; R52 gives precise capacity figures for a new on-site childcare center ('116 children... nine classrooms... two outdoor yards') that affects only Salesforce's own employees. Compare R40, whose numeric figures (70 million individuals) describe direct external consequence.

proposals.name: Warm in-group community-address voice
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text speaks directly and warmly to a specific in-group audience using relational, family-style framing (e.g. 'our community,' 'our Ohana,' 'Dear Host,' 'Dear Guest,' inclusive first-person-plural language treating employees/customers/hosts as partners or family). Score only the extent of this address style. Do not judge whether the sentiment expressed is sincere, good, or well-executed.
proposals.rationale: R08 and R14 (Salesforce 'Ohana' framing) and R22 (Airbnb 'Dear Host') carry very high card_pct (.956/.993/.962) despite thin hard-news content; this relational-address habit is a rhetorical practice of certain comms teams, not itself a measure of whether an independent journalist would judge the item worth writing up.
proposals.upstream_parent: internal comms / community-relations team's house style of audience address

proposals.name: Consumer promo listicle / how-to formatting
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text is structured as consumer shopping/how-to content: itemized deal terms, 'here's how to' framing, imperative tips-list phrasing, or an interview/Q&A layout with named spokespeople answering questions. Score only the presence of this structural format. Do not judge whether the promotion or advice is appealing, useful, or well-priced.
proposals.rationale: R02 (Green Monday percent-off deal terms) and R41 (Hatchimal availability 'tips' list) are both built around itemized promotional instructions rather than a reportable event; R56's Q&A layout with 'Joe P.:' / 'Joe C.:' follows the same interview-format habit. The listicle/how-to shape is a marketing-copy convention, not a newsworthiness signal.
proposals.upstream_parent: consumer-marketing team's promotional-copy format practice

proposals.name: Garbled or truncated extraction-artifact text
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the visible text shows mechanical extraction or truncation residue: an abrupt mid-word or mid-sentence cutoff with no terminal punctuation, stray code/markup fragments, or explicit meta-commentary describing 'the provided page content' rather than being press-release prose itself. Score only the presence of these mechanical artifacts. Do not judge whether the underlying announcement, where legible, is interesting.
proposals.rationale: R21 is not press-release prose at all but leftover scraper/meta commentary ('The provided raw page content does not appear to contain a press release or news article') and still carries a high card_pct (.962) against a low dense_pct (.263); R39 and R56 both cut off mid-word ('...the pipeli', '...warm and invit') rather than at a natural boundary, the same pipeline-artifact fingerprint.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Named senior-executive personal signature/byline
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how explicitly the text is framed as personally authored or signed by one named, senior individual: a byline with title, a first-person narrative sustained throughout, or a sign-off using a first name/initial. Score only the presence of this authorial framing. Do not judge whether the named individual's argument or news is compelling.
proposals.rationale: R16 closes with a first-name sign-off ('-- Elon') and R43 opens 'By Elizabeth Pinkham, EVP Global Real Estate'; R29 closes with an explicit named-and-titled byline ('Cindy Robbins is EVP, Global Employee Success'). A senior insider's personal account (as in R16's fire incident) could genuinely carry more real information, so this factor plausibly also drives true newsworthiness, not just scorer bias.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's seniority and personal practice of signing communications

proposals.name: Self-referential organizational scale superlatives
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text cites the issuing organization's own scale, reach, or record-breaking superlatives about itself, such as 'the most X in our history,' membership/user counts, 'world's largest/first/fastest,' or global market-count claims. Score only the extent of such self-referential scale claims. Do not judge whether the underlying achievement is actually significant.
proposals.rationale: R01 stacks self-superlatives ('the most amazing quarter in our history... most mind-blowing growth in the history of the automotive industry') and R13 cites '300 million guest arrivals... path to more than 1 billion annual guests by 2028'; R50 cites '6 million listings worldwide.' Genuine scale can correlate with real magnitude of news, so this branding habit may also be entangled with true newsworthiness.
proposals.upstream_parent: organizational size/prominence and media-relations following

proposals.name: Legal/regulatory compliance citation boilerplate
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text contains formal legal or regulatory compliance language: named statutes or rules, agency names with docket/filing references, disclaimers about what the release does or does not constitute, or procedural legal deadlines. Score only the presence of this compliance register. Do not judge whether the underlying legal matter is important.
proposals.rationale: R10 (Airbnb's confidential S-1 announcement) is built almost entirely around a Securities Act Rule 135 disclaimer, and R37 (Tesla's annual-meeting notice) is dense with proxy control-number and voting procedure text; R07 (mine-safety litigation update) is similarly procedural-filing prose. This register reflects counsel-driven drafting practice, not the intrinsic newsworthiness of the announcement.
proposals.upstream_parent: legal/compliance drafting process and counsel involvement

proposals.name: Reactive defensive crisis-incident narration
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text is structured as a defensive rebuttal to an external allegation, or as a blow-by-blow account of a specific dated incident/emergency (e.g. 'this petition is completely false,' minute-by-minute timelines, point-by-point refutation of a claim). Score only the presence of this reactive/defensive structure. Do not judge whether the defense is persuasive or the incident is serious.
proposals.rationale: R42 opens by flatly rebutting a petition ('This petition is completely false') and R59 rebuts a discrimination lawsuit point-by-point; R30 narrates a trespassing/assault incident with a timestamp ('Last Friday at approximately 11:50 am'). Controversy and breaking incidents are also classic drivers of genuine newsworthiness, so this timing factor is plausibly mixed rather than pure nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing under reactive/defensive pressure (crisis-response cadence)

proposals.name: Raw internal-memo/email header formatting
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text preserves raw internal-communication formatting: explicit email header fields ('From:', 'Sent:', 'To:', 'Subject:'), framing language like 'the following email was sent to employees,' or informal internal salutations, as opposed to prose written from the outset as an external press release. Score only the presence of this raw-memo formatting. Do not judge whether the leaked/republished content itself is important.
proposals.rationale: R16 embeds a literal email exchange with header fields ('From: robert Carlson / Sent: Thursday, October 03, 2013... / Subject: carlson 0389'); R01 and R23 (identical text) are explicitly framed as 'The following email was just sent to Tesla employees' rather than as an external release. Leaked/republished internal communications are often considered more newsworthy precisely because they are unfiltered, so this channel factor is plausibly mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: internal-vs-external communication channel / production process

proposals.name: Recurring periodic-series template positioning
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text presupposes it is one instalment in an established, recurring periodic series -- for example referencing 'the previous month,' citing a multi-year running data series, or following a rigid month-over-month/year-over-year template with only the figures changed -- rather than introducing a topic from scratch. Score only the extent of this recurring-instalment framing. Do not judge whether the specific data reported is noteworthy.
proposals.rationale: R03, R19, and R28 are three separate monthly S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller releases sharing near-identical boilerplate ('today released the latest results... More than 27 years of history are available'), differing mainly in the numbers. Novelty-versus-routineness is arguably part of genuine journalistic newsworthiness itself, so this container-position marker may be entangled with true newsworthiness rather than a pure nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream / recurring periodic series

proposals.name: Formal wire-service dateline/distribution convention
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text opens with formal wire-service dateline conventions: an ALL-CAPS city name followed by a date, an explicit wire-service credit (e.g. '/PRNewswire/'), or a colon-terminated dateline preceding the lead sentence, as opposed to an undated first-person 'company blog' opening. Score only the presence of this dateline/distribution formatting. Do not judge whether the story behind it is important.
proposals.rationale: R15 opens with a full wire-service dateline and explicit credit ('TEANECK, N.J. and LONDON, Oct. 4, 2012 / PRNewswire / --') and R49 opens 'MINNEAPOLIS - January 10, 2014'; R03/R19/R28 all open 'NEW YORK, [DATE]:' in the same wire convention. Paid-newswire distribution may correlate with genuinely larger corporate events, so this format marker is plausibly mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: distribution tier / paid newswire vs owned-channel publishing practice

proposals.name: Public-impact breadth
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text describes consequential effects on a broad public, community, market, infrastructure, or civic domain; score 0 when it concerns only internal audiences, routine customers, or brand image.
proposals.rationale: R32 describes exposure involving up to 70 million people, while R50 concerns nationwide fuel pricing and household costs.

proposals.name: Cross-institutional coordination
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when named outside organizations have defined, substantive roles in a shared mechanism or initiative; score 0 when partners are merely mentioned or the organization acts alone.
proposals.rationale: R06 involves manufacturers, charging operators, and standards bodies, while R45 describes Airbnb and Vrbo building a shared third-party process.

proposals.name: Non-routine change
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text documents a clear break from prior policy, operating practice, product capability, or organizational model; score 0 when it describes continuity, generic values, routine hiring, or an ordinary promotion.
proposals.rationale: R20 describes a platform-wide policy shift and R36 converts an in-person event into an online format, unlike routine material in R02 and R14.

proposals.name: Immediate audience actionability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when readers receive a specific, material public-facing action or access change with concrete timing, location, conditions, or channels; score 0 when the text offers only aspiration, vague invitation, or a sales promotion.
proposals.rationale: R10 gives specific urban charging locations and charging behavior, while R58 supplies reservation channels, regional sequencing, and production timing.

proposals.name: Measurable technical novelty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a new technical capability is supported by quantitative benchmarks, comparison points, and an explained mechanism; score 0 when claims rely mainly on unsupported superlatives or promotional adjectives.
proposals.rationale: R18 supplies battery, aerodynamic, and range measurements, while R54 details cameras, sensors, computing power, and system capabilities.

proposals.name: Incident specificity and severity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text reports a concrete incident with identifiable timing, location, people or systems involved, harm or exposure, and response; score 0 when no specific incident is described.
proposals.rationale: R16 gives detailed vehicle-fire circumstances and containment, while R24 describes a trespass incident, injuries, vehicles, and law-enforcement involvement.

proposals.name: Contested accountability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when named parties present conflicting accounts, allegations, or responsibilities involving legal, regulatory, safety, or institutional stakes; score 0 when the text contains no substantive disagreement.
proposals.rationale: R12 describes opposing positions over mine-safety enforcement, while R13 sets Tesla’s account against a state agency’s discrimination allegations.

proposals.name: Quantified trend significance
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text presents a measured change over time against a baseline and explains its broader sector or public significance; score 0 when it gives only an isolated figure or an ungrounded estimate.
proposals.rationale: R11 and R17 compare housing-price movements across periods and regions, while R21 documents a multi-year vehicle-age trend with supply-chain context.

proposals.name: Material scale and stakes
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when amounts, populations, geographic scope, usage, or operational capacity are large enough to materially raise the subject’s significance; score 0 when scale is absent or expressed only as vague terms such as “global.”
proposals.rationale: R38 specifies a $1 billion investment, while R56 specifies $250 million in host support and a $10 million relief fund.

proposals.name: Social issue plus concrete practice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a socially salient issue is tied to specific operational practices, resources, eligibility, or measurable implementation; score 0 when the text consists mainly of values statements or symbolic language.
proposals.rationale: R03 links pay equity to salary analysis and adjustments, while R31 links racial justice to a holiday, pay treatment, and organizational action.

proposals.name: Human-interest access
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text offers unusual access to identifiable people, vivid settings, direct testimony, or a concrete personal experience; score 0 when it remains impersonal and abstract.
proposals.rationale: R49 centers on Seth Rogen hosting guests in a distinctive creative space, while R16 includes correspondence with the owner involved in the vehicle fire.

proposals.name: Credible implementation path
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when forward-looking claims include named milestones, dates, responsible actors, deliverables, and relevant constraints; score 0 when future language is aspirational without a schedule or mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R18 provides a demonstration plan, upgrade timing, and safety-validation constraint, while R26 specifies twenty destinations and the planned structure of their hubs.

proposals.name: Independent evidentiary grounding
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when claims are supported by named datasets, regulators, court records, experts, witnesses, or technical measurements; score 0 when the text relies exclusively on issuer assertions and testimonials.
proposals.rationale: R37 attributes detailed trade figures to China’s customs authority, while R42 cites border officials, airline representatives, and a passenger account.

proposals.name: Substance over promotion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when neutral facts, context, limitations, and operational detail dominate the text; score 0 when slogans, self-praise, calls to buy or watch, and brand boilerplate dominate.
proposals.rationale: R01 and R44 are chiefly celebratory or promotional, while R11 and R12 devote substantial space to data, context, and institutional particulars.

proposals.name: Adverse-fact candor
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the issuer openly presents harmful, embarrassing, risky, or legally exposed facts with concrete scope, uncertainty, and response; score 0 when adverse information is absent or replaced by vague reassurance.
proposals.rationale: R05 discloses payment-card exposure with dates and affected information, while R39 openly reports weaker-than-expected sales and investor concern.

proposals.name: Encoding and markup artifacts
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of malformed encoding, stray characters, raw markup, missing text, or layout corruption visible in the item; do not judge whether this is good, bad, credible, or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Rendering damage can affect text processing without conveying news value. Visible examples include corrupted apostrophes and missing spaces in R09 and R41, stray “A” artifacts in R15, and an effectively empty payload in R55.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Promotional superlative density
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of celebratory hype, exaggerated superlatives, exclamation, and promotional intensifiers; do not judge whether the claims or style are good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Some authors use highly promotional language as a routine house style, which can attract attention independently of news value. R05 contains “most mind-blowing growth” and “insanely badass,” while R31 uses “wellness winner,” “oh-so much,” and “how awesome is that?!”.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format

proposals.name: Community-address intimacy
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of direct address, first-person relationship language, named community identities, and conversational appeals to readers; do not judge whether this relationship-building is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: An organisation’s established audience can shape its communication voice and reception, while also sometimes relating to genuine public interest. R18 addresses hosts as partners throughout, and R22 directly addresses “Boutique Hotel and Bed and Breakfast Owners” with community-oriented language.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience/following

proposals.name: Quantitative and technical density
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of numerical tables, percentages, measurements, formulas, named indices, and technical specifications; do not judge whether the detail is useful, accurate, or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Dense figures and specifications can make text appear authoritative or information-rich without establishing independent news value. R45 is dominated by import tables and percentage changes, while R12 provides repeated index values, city rankings, and historical-series detail.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Newswire release scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of formal wire-service conventions such as all-caps datelines, ticker symbols, distribution labels, standardized lead wording, and corporate boilerplate; do not judge whether the format is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Major-wire or syndicated distribution leaves recognizable formatting traces that can affect reception independently of substance. R30 includes “/ PRNewswire /,” ticker symbols, datelines, and an “About” section; R12 and R20 use standardized all-caps location-and-date leads for recurring data releases.
proposals.upstream_parent: distribution tier

proposals.name: Agency-style announcement formula
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of polished PR architecture: benefit-led headlines, subheads, quote blocks, repeated key takeaways, list sections, calls to action, and standardized company descriptions; do not judge whether the packaging is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Outside drafting or intensive communications editing can leave a formulaic structure that attracts attention, and the same assistance may sometimes improve substantive communication. R30 uses a benefit subhead, multiple executive quotes, and an “About” section; R40 repeats key takeaways and combines lists, quotations, and promotional boilerplate.
proposals.upstream_parent: drafting or editing assistance

proposals.name: Owned-channel engagement cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of newsroom or marketing-page cues such as subscription prompts, “learn more” links, booking instructions, FAQs, customer-service directions, and promotional calls to action; do not judge whether these cues are good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Owned-channel publication leaves engagement infrastructure in the text, which can shape textual reception without indicating independent news value. R03 directs readers to an FAQ and future updates, while R10 contains booking instructions, host links, eligibility notes, and promotional discovery links.
proposals.upstream_parent: distribution tier

proposals.name: Series-continuity presupposition
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent to which the item presupposes earlier releases, continues a named programme, reports another periodic installment, or uses “update,” “earlier,” and “following” language; do not judge whether the continuation is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: An item’s unseen position in an organisation’s release sequence can leave textual continuity markers that affect interpretation without changing the underlying news value. R20 and R42 are recurring Case-Shiller installments with month-over-month comparisons; R49 explicitly refers back to the August 2020 temporary ban.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Calendar and news-cycle cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of explicit dates, quarter-end references, holiday or shopping-season language, event timing, embargo-like conventions, and crisis-period references; do not judge whether the timing is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Submission timing can affect attention and can also coincide with genuinely timely events, so the parent is plausibly mixed. R05 foregrounds the final weeks of a quarter, R14 is built around Green Monday and Christmas shopping, and R52 specifies a shareholder meeting and Battery Day schedule.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing

proposals.name: Prestige and celebrity name halo
