proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of references to celebrities, globally prominent companies, governments, major institutions, famous partners, or unusually large audience and reach claims; do not judge whether the named entities or associations are good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Institutional reputation and audience can affect reception while sometimes overlapping with genuine public interest, making this a mixed nuisance. R10 prominently features Seth Rogen and Airbnb, while R26 foregrounds UNESCO, Mexico City, and Airbnb; R08 similarly invokes Silver Lake and Sixth Street Partners.
proposals.upstream_parent: organisation prominence and audience/following

proposals.name: Unexpected news hook
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the release presents a surprising, easily summarized development that departs from ordinary corporate activity; score 0 when it is a routine update with no unusual angle.
proposals.rationale: The trespassing confrontation in R24, the celebrity-hosted creative retreat in R40, and the confidential IPO filing in R57 each contain an immediately recognizable hook that routine announcements lack.

proposals.name: Adversarial public conflict
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text describes a concrete dispute with a named regulator, institution, company, or identifiable opposing party; score 0 when no external disagreement or contested claim appears.
proposals.rationale: R03 responds to a petition and short-seller allegations, R12 confronts a state employment agency, and R28 describes litigation over mine-safety rules.

proposals.name: Vivid safety or security event
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the release gives a specific incident, causal sequence, and concrete threat to people, property, or public security; score 0 when safety language is generic or hypothetical.
proposals.rationale: R24 details injuries and vehicle movements, R33 describes 180 passengers passing without passport checks, and R51 explains a vehicle fire after a severe roadway collision.

proposals.name: Explicit scale of exposure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text clearly quantifies how many people, assets, locations, or jurisdictions are directly involved; score 0 when the affected population or geographic scope is absent or purely vague.
proposals.rationale: R25 names up to 70 million individuals, R13 specifies 160 locations and 50,000 employees, and R01 defines a bounded population and date range.

proposals.name: Record or benchmark claim
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the release makes a specific, quantified comparison against a historical, industry, geographic, or product benchmark; score 0 when it offers only unquantified superlatives.
proposals.rationale: R07 and R17 compare acceleration and range with elite vehicles, while R37, R41, and R48 provide explicit market or engineering benchmarks.

proposals.name: Mechanism-linked capability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text explains both how a product or system works and what concrete user-facing capability follows; score 0 when it merely asserts benefits without a mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R08 explains charger architecture and charging times, R38 describes sensors and remote parking controls, and R49 details cameras, radar, sensors, and onboard computing.

proposals.name: Industry-wide interoperability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the announcement changes how multiple independent organisations, platforms, or systems can interoperate; score 0 when the change applies only within the issuing organisation.
proposals.rationale: R15 opens Tesla's connector design to manufacturers and networks, R58 creates cross-platform information sharing, and R47 combines Airbnb, UNESCO, and a city government.

proposals.name: Time-sensitive access
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text gives a near-term date, deadline, limited window, scarce quantity, or constrained access condition that makes the information immediately usable; score 0 when no timing or access constraint is specified.
proposals.rationale: R23 gives arrival dates and purchase limits, R40 offers only three one-night stays, and R50 specifies reservation timing and regional delivery sequencing.

proposals.name: Identifiable human protagonist
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a named non-executive person or clearly identified participant performs an unusual, consequential, or firsthand role in the described event; score 0 when people appear only as generic customers, employees, or quoted officials.
proposals.rationale: R40 makes Seth Rogen the host and hands-on participant, R24 identifies journalists and security personnel in the incident, and R51 includes firsthand correspondence from the vehicle owner.

proposals.name: Concrete policy or legal mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the release explains a specific rule, legal proceeding, regulatory change, or enforcement mechanism and identifies who it governs; score 0 when policy language is aspirational or lacks an operative mechanism.
proposals.rationale: R22 explains Spanish tax reporting and host tools, R28 describes the mine-safety enforcement rule and court briefing, and R36 specifies Nigeria's fuel-pricing regime.

proposals.name: Independent evidentiary grounding
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when important claims are supported by named external data sources, independent institutions, multiple attributable parties, or clearly described evidence; score 0 when claims rely only on the issuer's assertions.
proposals.rationale: R33 includes statements from three organisations, R37 cites the Case-Shiller index and long historical series, and R39 identifies China's customs authority and its conversion method.

proposals.name: Accountable disclosure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the issuer acknowledges uncertainty, criticism, failure, or competing claims and supplies specific facts, safeguards, or explanatory detail; score 0 when the text is entirely self-congratulatory and avoids adverse information.
proposals.rationale: R12 addresses allegations and missing factual details, R31 apologises for communication with hosts while specifying support measures, and R55 reports both safety improvements and remaining weaknesses.

proposals.name: Material benefit at broad scale
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the release specifies a substantial resource, payment, leave entitlement, facility, or service available to a clearly defined and sizable group; score 0 when benefits are symbolic, vague, or limited to general goodwill.
proposals.rationale: R30 specifies a company holiday, pay treatment, and a $10 million commitment, R31 names $250 million and $10 million support funds, and R04 details paid leave and caregiving benefits.

proposals.name: Public-facing stakes
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the described change bears directly on public safety, markets, infrastructure, regulation, consumers, or communities beyond the issuer's insiders; score 0 when it mainly concerns internal culture, branding, routine merchandising, or employee perks.
proposals.rationale: R25 concerns consumer data for up to 70 million people and R36 concerns national fuel prices, whereas R16 and R04 primarily describe internal employee benefits.

proposals.name: Editorially usable completeness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the text independently supplies a clear subject, actors, timing, location or scope, concrete particulars, and a concise central proposition; score 0 when it is mostly promotional filler, fragmented content, or lacks an identifiable announcement.
proposals.rationale: R25 and R50 provide self-contained facts, dates, actors, and practical particulars, while R45 lacks an identifiable release body and R27 offers little beyond a celebratory claim.

proposals.name: Reused passage or update
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the text reproduces earlier wording or repeats sections; judge only textual reuse, not whether it is good, important, or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Repeated or republished wording can reflect workflow and template reuse rather than news value. The duplicated Target notices in R03, R05, and R59, and repeated key takeaways in R16, show this trace.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing and publication reuse process

proposals.name: Encoding or extraction damage
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the text contains malformed characters, missing spaces, broken markup, HTML artifacts, or visibly corrupted extraction; do not judge whether the feature is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Technical corruption can affect model perception while saying nothing about journalistic value. Examples include the malformed punctuation and spacing in R26 and R32, and the damaged presentation in R42 and R33.
proposals.upstream_parent: content-ingest or export pipeline

proposals.name: Direct executive-message voice
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the item uses a first-person executive or employee-message format, direct address, email framing, or a personal sign-off; judge only the extent of this voice, not its quality or newsworthiness.
proposals.rationale: Direct messages may receive attention because of communication practice or audience expectations, independently of the underlying news. R14 and R30 begin as emails to Tesla employees, while R19 and R36 reproduce leadership messages to employees or hosts.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice and intended audience

proposals.name: Adversarial rebuttal framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the text denies allegations, attacks or characterizes an opposing party, invokes legal proceedings, or presents a defensive counter-narrative; judge only the extent of this framing, not whether it is justified or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Defensive communications can attract attention because of the response process itself, while the wording need not indicate independent news value. R20, R40, R47, and R07 use conspicuous rebuttal, accusation, or incident-response framing.
proposals.upstream_parent: crisis-response and media-scrutiny process

proposals.name: Playful brand voice
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the text uses playful slang, jokes, exclamation, whimsical metaphors, fan language, or an entertainment-oriented promotional persona; do not judge whether that style is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: A brand's audience strategy can produce attention-grabbing language unrelated to journalistic importance. R01 uses wordplay around Green Monday, R24 uses enthusiastic lifestyle language, and R45 and R46 use playful consumer-facing phrasing.
proposals.upstream_parent: marketing and audience-engagement practice

proposals.name: Structured industry data template
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the item follows a standardized market-data template with formal index names, recurring period comparisons, dense figures, units, tables, or source notes; judge only the extent of the template, not the value of the findings.
proposals.rationale: Recurring analytical formats can be mistaken for importance because they are dense and authoritative-looking. R21, R28, and R55 use nearly identical housing-index structures, while R27 and R02 use highly templated commodity or vehicle-fleet reporting.
proposals.upstream_parent: industry data-release practice

proposals.name: Series-presupposition language
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the text presupposes earlier coverage through words such as update, codify, continue, build on, following, or previously announced; judge only the extent of that textual presupposition, not whether the item is newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: An item's place in an organizational series can shape reception, and first announcements versus routine continuations may also correlate with genuine news value. R16 codifies a previously temporary policy, R18 follows related country announcements, and R13 builds on an earlier initiative.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Calendar and event-timing markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the text contains explicit dates, deadlines, quarter or earnings references, holiday timing, event times, embargo-style wording, or immediate-release conventions; do not judge whether the timing is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Calendar placement and release conventions can affect visibility without changing the content's intrinsic journalistic value. R01 and R45 emphasize holiday shopping windows, while R14, R23, and R39 foreground quarter-end or scheduled-event timing.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing and news-cycle conventions

proposals.name: Wire and disclosure boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the text contains datelines, stock tickers, PR-wire labels, formal About sections, securities disclaimers, metadata bylines, or regulatory safe-harbor language; judge only the extent of these markers, not whether they are useful or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Newswire or owned-newsroom packaging can create a reception prior independent of the substance. R34 visibly carries PRNewswire and ticker boilerplate, R37 contains an SEC Rule 135 disclaimer, and R51 uses platform metadata and repeated key-takeaway packaging.
proposals.upstream_parent: distribution tier and communications channel

proposals.name: Transactional call-to-action density
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the text gives purchase, booking, reservation, enrollment, pricing, discount, URL, or store-visit instructions; judge only the amount of transactional direction, not whether the offer is good or newsworthy.
proposals.rationale: Conversion-oriented copy can be prominent because of campaign objectives rather than independent news value. R01 gives discount mechanics, R23 gives reservation procedures, R45 gives purchase guidance, and R60 details ordering and leasing actions.
proposals.upstream_parent: marketing and conversion workflow

proposals.name: Quantitative Specificity Over Vague Claims
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text supports its major claims with precise, exact numerical figures, dates, or percentages; score 0 if the text contains no metrics and relies entirely on qualitative adjectives.
proposals.rationale: Dense models recognize that hard, specific data points (R01, R58) are what journalists actually need, whereas scorecards over-credit releases with vague, unquantified corporate fluff (R10, R18).

proposals.name: Factual Refutation of External Allegations
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text directly, point-by-point refutes a specific external accusation, lawsuit, or crisis with hard data; score 0 if it ignores the issue or relies purely on generic apologies.
proposals.rationale: Dense models assign high value to fact-based pushback against controversies (R09, R52), while scorecards miss this and over-credit boilerplate crisis responses that lack substantive defense (R03, R06).

proposals.name: Comparative Benchmarking Together With Quantitative Evidence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text explicitly compares the announcement to specific named competitors or historical baselines using numbers; score 0 if it discusses products or initiatives in a vacuum.
proposals.rationale: Journalists need context, which is why dense-high items benchmark achievements against known entities (R04, R58), whereas scorecard-high items often lack any comparative context (R25, R60).

proposals.name: Verbatim Disclosure of Primary Sources
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text publishes original, verbatim documents, direct internal emails, or primary communications; score 0 if it contains only highly polished, synthesized PR statements.
proposals.rationale: Dense models heavily weight the inclusion of actual internal texts (R01, R12) because they provide unfiltered evidence, unlike standard synthesized PR disguised as direct communication (R23, R46).

proposals.name: Disruptive Industry Firsts or Market-Defining Actions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text announces a definitive industry first, a record-breaking metric, or a new structural standard; score 0 if it announces a routine, incremental corporate update.
proposals.rationale: Dense models capture the massive news value of unprecedented shifts (R11, R37), whereas scorecards miss the historical context and over-credit routine internal programs (R28, R56).

proposals.name: Strategic Rationale Together With Acknowledged Trade-offs
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text transparently explains the business logic of a decision while explicitly acknowledging a downside, delay, or limitation; score 0 if it is purely promotional with zero caveats.
proposals.rationale: Dense models value the credibility created by transparent reasoning and admitted trade-offs (R24, R37), while scorecards are easily fooled by one-sided, purely promotional releases (R10, R48).

proposals.name: Direct Executive Voice and Unconventional Phrasing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text is written with a strong, distinct, unfiltered voice characteristic of a specific leader; score 0 if it uses generic, sterile corporate boilerplate.
proposals.rationale: Authentic, colorful executive quotes signal high news value to dense models (R12, R55), whereas scorecards fail to distinguish this from highly sanitized corporate-speak (R05, R18).

proposals.name: External Macro-Context Together With Direct Company Action
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text explicitly connects a major macroeconomic or societal shift to a specific, newly announced company action; score 0 if it is hyper-focused on internal news without broader context.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high items successfully frame company news as part of major global trends (R08, R57), while scorecard-high items remain myopically focused on internal updates (R13, R32).

proposals.name: Tangible Public Calls to Action Together With Exact Logistics
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text provides concrete dates, exact pricing, or specific URLs for the public to act immediately; score 0 if it contains vague future promises with no actionable details.
proposals.rationale: Dense models favor releases that give consumers immediate, actionable logistics (R21, R38), whereas scorecards over-credit releases lacking any immediate public action (R10, R25).

proposals.name: Hard Economic or Market Data over Subjective Philanthropy
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text releases objective, hard economic indices or audited market data; score 0 if it focuses on subjective, unverifiable corporate philanthropy or internal CSR goals.
proposals.rationale: Dense models heavily favor the release of objective, hard economic indices (R44, R51), whereas scorecards over-credit soft, unverifiable philanthropy announcements (R29, R35).

proposals.name: Third-Party Institutional Validation of Claims
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text validates its announcement via formal partnerships with credible external institutions, government bodies, or named experts; score 0 if it is entirely self-referential.
proposals.rationale: Dense models assign higher value to claims that are independently validated by credible external bodies (R08, R36) compared to self-praising corporate assertions (R18, R46).

proposals.name: Definitive Changes to Product Ecosystems or Infrastructure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text announces major, structural changes to physical products, software ecosystems, or public infrastructure; score 0 if it announces minor cosmetic changes or routine policies.
proposals.rationale: Dense models rank announcements of major infrastructure shifts highly (R11, R58), whereas scorecards miss the scale and over-credit minor operational updates (R60) or internal benefits (R13).

proposals.name: Authorial Transparency About the Medium
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text explicitly references the format of the message itself (e.g., 'The following email was sent'); score 0 if it reads as an undated, contextless promotional flyer.
proposals.rationale: Contextualizing the text as a leaked or direct internal communication signals high news value to the dense model (R01, R12) versus static promotional flyers lacking context (R05, R25).

proposals.name: Clear Depiction of Stakeholder Conflict or Tension
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text highlights a clear, specific conflict between the organization and an identifiable antagonist; score 0 if it presents a sanitized, conflict-free narrative.
proposals.rationale: Dense models heavily weight clear adversarial tension or investigative drama (R09, R55), which scorecards miss, instead over-crediting sanitized, generic conflict-free narratives (R03, R06).

proposals.name: Specificity of Downstream Consumer Impact
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the text details exactly how the announcement will change the daily lives or finances of specific consumer groups; score 0 if it focuses abstractly on corporate values.
proposals.rationale: Dense models value clear explanations of how new rules immediately impact end-users (R04, R24), while scorecards over-credit abstract internal goals (R18, R28).

proposals.name: Internal Comm Repackaging
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text explicitly frames itself as a leaked or shared internal message directed at a specific internal audience (e.g., using phrases like 'The following email was sent to employees...', 'Dear Host', or 'Dear Target Guest'). Judge the extent of this framing only; do not judge whether it is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: Items like R05 and R09 are framed as internal letters ('The following email was just sent to Tesla employees', 'Below is an email... sent to Airbnb hosts'). R31, R41, and R48 are addressed directly to 'Dear Target Guest'. This format signals a dedicated, pre-existing audience and often generates high engagement, skewing dense model perceptions regardless of broad newsworthiness.
proposals.upstream_parent: PR strategy / bypassing wires to use owned audience

proposals.name: Executive Cult-of-Personality Tone
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text features highly informal, first-person, subjective, or hyperbolic language characteristic of a prominent founder or CEO, rather than standard corporate PR tone. Judge the extent of this stylistic voice only; do not judge whether the voice is effective or good.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R60 use phrases like 'insanely badass' and 'mind-blowing growth'. This distinctive tone (e.g., Elon Musk's voice) strongly predicts independent media pickup because of the individual's established following, making the release highly newsworthy to the dense model even if the underlying corporate event (a management reshuffle) is relatively routine.
proposals.upstream_parent: Author's practice in the format / CEO seniority and following

proposals.name: Scraped Web Page Artifacts
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text contains raw web formatting, HTML artifacts, UI instructions, or broken text from a web scrape (e.g., 'Key Takeaways', 'Not registered?', or 'Sign up to receive updates'). Judge the extent of these artifacts only; do not judge the quality of the underlying text.
proposals.rationale: R03 contains broken HTML and scraped marketing copy ('The provided raw page content does not appear...'), while R34 includes paywall text ('Not registered? Receive daily email alerts...'). This is a nuisance fingerprint of the distribution tier or ingestion process that artificially dilutes the readable content.
proposals.upstream_parent: Distribution tier / scraping process

proposals.name: Dense Technical Specifications
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text is dominated by highly granular numerical specifications, engineering acronyms, and scientific terminology. Judge the extent of the technical jargon only; do not judge whether the specifications are accurate or good.
proposals.rationale: R14 and R51 are saturated with metrics like 'Cd of 0.36', 'Crr of 11.0 kg/ton', and '72 kilowatts'. This fingerprints an engineering-led drafting process. Dense models may heavily weight this specialized, data-rich text, interpreting it as high signal, whereas scorecard models may penalize it for lacking traditional PR quotes or narrative flow.
proposals.upstream_parent: Author's practice in the format (engineer vs PR writer)

proposals.name: Recurring Calendar Data Report
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text positions itself as the latest installment in a routine, recurring data series or regular calendar update (e.g., using phrases like 'latest results for the', 'preliminary data released on Tuesday'). Judge the extent of this routine positioning only; do not judge the importance of the data.
proposals.rationale: R13, R20, and R21 all open with near-identical language: 'today released the latest results for the S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller Indices... More than 27 years of history are available'. This is a fingerprint of a recurring institutional calendar update. The dense model perceives these as highly newsworthy data drops, while the scorecard may view them as routine.
proposals.upstream_parent: Position in the entry stream / news cycle

proposals.name: Employer Branding and CSR Jargon
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text focuses on internal employee wellness, benefits, diversity, sustainability, or corporate philanthropy using qualitative, community-oriented language. Judge the extent of this HR/CSR focus only; do not judge whether the initiatives are good.
proposals.rationale: R04, R46, R50, and R59 are filled with CSR jargon ('core beliefs', 'equality a core value', 'wellbeing is one of our values'). Scorecards often reward these texts for hitting structural criteria and positive corporate narratives, but the dense model discounts them because working journalists rarely write up routine employer branding as independent news.
proposals.upstream_parent: Corporate comms goal (brand building vs. news)

proposals.name: Direct Marketing Call-To-Action
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text functions as a retail or marketing circular, containing explicit calls to action to buy products, reserve tickets, or use promo codes. Judge the extent of the promotional calls-to-action only; do not judge the attractiveness of the offer.
proposals.rationale: R07 uses explicit promotional language ('Save $20 for every $100 you spend'), and R27 asks consumers to 'get your hands on one' regarding Hatchimals. R56 contains detailed booking instructions. This is a surface fingerprint of a marketing department drafting the release rather than PR, which strongly skews scorecard metrics but does not reflect journalistic newsworthiness.
proposals.upstream_parent: Marketing distribution vs. PR distribution

proposals.name: Defensive Legal Posturing
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text is structured as a defensive rebuttal to a lawsuit, accident, or regulatory action, using combative language against external critics. Judge the extent of the defensive posture only; do not judge whether the defense is justified.
proposals.rationale: R22 ('petition is completely false') and R25 ('appears focused on alleged misconduct') are highly defensive legal rebuttals. Their combative, urgent tone strongly correlates with journalistic coverage (making them newsworthy to the dense model), but they may lack the standard positive PR structure the scorecard expects.
proposals.upstream_parent: Crisis management process / legal involvement

proposals.name: Corpus Duplication / Repetition
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text appears to be a verbatim duplicate or heavily syndicated copy of another release in the exact same format, lacking any original phrasing for its specific issuance. Judge the extent of the formulaic duplication only; do not judge the quality of the content.
proposals.rationale: R31, R41, and R48 are completely identical Target data breach letters. R05 and R60 are identical Tesla emails. A model may score the exact same text multiple times in completely opposite ways depending on the presence of other surface features, creating artificial extremes in the disagreement pool.
proposals.upstream_parent: Distribution / syndication tier

proposals.name: Trade Publication Journalistic Style
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text reads like a finished news article or industry newsletter rather than a press release, featuring reporter attributions, analyst quotes, and subscriber prompts. Judge the extent of this journalistic style only; do not judge the article's quality.
proposals.rationale: R19 and R29 are written as standard S&P Global Platts trade articles ('analysts at Keefe Bruyette & Woods', 'Singapore --'). R37 includes journalistic attribution ('Airport International understands'). These are already news stories masquerading as press releases in the corpus, which inherently confounds a dense model trying to evaluate 'how newsworthy' the release is.
proposals.upstream_parent: Distribution tier (news organization vs. corporate PR)

proposals.name: Adversarial Engagement with Named External Party
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release takes a clear combative, defensive, or refutational stance against a specifically named external entity (regulator, media outlet, competitor, activist, petitioner). Score 0 if the release is purely cooperative, celebratory, or neutral with no named oppositional party.
proposals.rationale: The dense model consistently elevates releases that confront named adversaries. R01 bluntly calls a petition 'completely false' and names the short-seller behind it; R36 attacks the California DFEH by name and questions its credibility. The scorecard likely lacks a dimension for adversarial energy, which journalists find inherently newsworthy.

proposals.name: Verifiable Record or 'First-Ever' Claim
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release makes a specific, testable claim of being first, fastest, longest-range, highest-rated, or unprecedented in a way a journalist could verify or cite. Score 0 if the release makes no comparative or superlative claim.
proposals.rationale: R08/R23 claims the Model S P100D is the 'third fastest accelerating production car ever produced' and 'first to go beyond 300 miles'; R20 announces an 'official EPA-rated range of 402 miles.' These are concrete, citable records. R49 and R52 make no such testable claims yet score high on the card.

proposals.name: Quantitative Head-to-Head Competitive Benchmark
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release provides specific numerical comparisons against named competitors, industry averages, or alternative technologies. Score 0 if the release makes only self-referential claims with no external comparison.
proposals.rationale: R18 compares fire rates (1 per 100M miles for Tesla vs. 1 per 20M miles for gasoline cars) and combustion energy (10% of a comparable gasoline tank); R16 compares Tesla's TRIR to both the industry average and the prior NUMMI operator. These comparisons give journalists ready-made story angles the scorecard may not detect.

proposals.name: Vivid Physical or Technical Event Detail
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release includes precise, granular physical, sensory, or engineering details that let a reader visualise what happened (measurements, forces, sequences, materials). Score 0 if events are described only in vague, abstract terms.
proposals.rationale: R05 describes specific injuries ('approximate 2" bleeding laceration to his right forearm') and vehicle dynamics ('put it in reverse and accelerated into the Tesla employee'); R18 specifies 'a peak force on the order of 25 tons' punching 'a 3 inch diameter hole through the quarter inch armor plate.' This specificity signals genuine news. Contrast with R39/R55, which use only generic language about a breach.

proposals.name: Insider Communication Access Framing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release is explicitly framed as an internal communication (employee email, private letter, leaked memo) shared with the public, giving the reader a sense of privileged access. Score 0 if the release is a standard outward-facing corporate statement with no insider framing.
proposals.rationale: R06/R44 are introduced as 'The following email was just sent to Tesla employees'; R18 reprints private email correspondence with the vehicle owner 'with his permission.' This 'you-are-there' quality is inherently compelling to journalists but may not register on a criterion checklist.

proposals.name: Actionable Consumer Transaction Pathway
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release provides concrete pricing, dates, locations, and steps a consumer can immediately act on (reserve, purchase, upgrade, lease). Score 0 if the release mentions products or services without specific actionable details.
proposals.rationale: R19 tells consumers exactly when, where, and how to reserve a Model 3, including reservation amounts by currency; R42 specifies exact prices ($37,500 → $39,500), lease terms, and mileage options. R03 also mentions a sale but superficially—no specific product prices, just a spend-and-save formula. The dense model appears to distinguish real transactional specificity from promotional fluff.

proposals.name: Independent Institutional Data Authority
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release's primary value comes from data or findings issued by, or formally attributed to, a named independent institution with established methodological authority. Score 0 if all claims are self-reported by the issuing company with no external institutional backing.
proposals.rationale: R07/R33/R59 are S&P Dow Jones Indices releases of the Case-Shiller data—the authoritative source for US home prices. R58 (S&P Global Mobility on vehicle ages) also has this quality but scores dense_low, suggesting the dense model also weighs concision (see A14). Still, institutional data authority helps explain why R07/R33/R59 rank so high on the dense model but low on a scorecard that may not credit source provenance.

proposals.name: Dramatic Narrative with Escalating Stakes
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release tells a story with a clear arc of conflict, escalation, and consequences—rising tension, a turning point, and a resolution with real-world impact. Score 0 if the release has no narrative arc and merely lists facts or announcements.
proposals.rationale: R05 builds from trespassing discovery → confrontation → vehicle assault → arrest, a natural news story; R14 tracks Apple's earnings miss → 10% stock drop → analyst commentary → production-cut rumours. R47 (a Q&A about store remodels) has no dramatic arc whatsoever, yet scores high on the card.

proposals.name: Distinctive Executive Voice with Personality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release features a strong, recognisable individual voice using idiosyncratic language, informal phrasing, or personal asides that signal authentic authorship. Score 0 if all quoted or narrative language is corporate-generic and could have been written by any PR department.
proposals.rationale: R06/R44 includes 'That is insanely badass' and an informal product-teasing 'And that's just what people know about...'; R18 is signed simply '--Elon' and uses direct, punchy technical prose. R49 is a generic CEO letter full of phrases like 'intrinsically linked to the health and vitality'—no personality at all.

proposals.name: Industry Structural Change Scope
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the announced change alters how an entire industry operates—a new standard, a cross-platform collaboration, or a move that forces competitors to respond. Score 0 if the announcement affects only the issuing company's internal operations or product line.
proposals.rationale: R54 opens Tesla's charging connector to all manufacturers and renames it the North American Charging Standard—a potential industry-wide shift; R13 announces the first cross-platform collaboration between Airbnb and Vrbo on shared safety enforcement. R56 announces a vendor alliance that changes nothing structurally, yet the scorecard rates both similarly.

proposals.name: Substantive Counter-Analysis in Crisis Response
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if, in responding to a negative event, the release provides genuine new technical analysis, causal explanation, comparative data, or investigative findings—not just reassurance or apology. Score 0 if the crisis response is limited to expressions of regret, vague reassurances, and formulaic promises to do better.
proposals.rationale: R18 explains exactly how the fire propagated, how the battery firewalls contained it, and provides comparative fire statistics; R01 provides pedal-misapplication data and Autopilot mitigation logic. R39/R55/R60 are near-identical boilerplate apology letters about the Target breach, providing no new technical information—yet the scorecard rates them highly. The dense model distinguishes substantive analysis from formulaic crisis PR.

proposals.name: Boilerplate-Free Directness of Language
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release uses direct, plain, sometimes blunt language throughout, avoiding corporate clichés, buzzword stacks, and formulaic structures. Score 0 if the release is dominated by standard corporate-PR phrases ('committed to,' 'proud to announce,' 'intrinsically linked,' 'lasting change').
proposals.rationale: R01 opens with 'This petition is completely false'—maximum directness; R05 is a plain factual account of an incident. R49 is dense with boilerplate ('intrinsically linked to the health and vitality,' 'active citizens and valued neighbors'); R22 deploys 'creating lasting change around racial justice and equity.' The scorecard may reward topic relevance while the dense model penalises formulaic packaging.

proposals.name: Previously Undisclosed Strategic Reveal
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release discloses a concrete future plan, product capability, or strategic direction that was not previously known publicly and that has clear implications. Score 0 if the release restates known commitments, reaffirms existing strategies, or describes only incremental refinements.
proposals.rationale: R35 reveals that all Teslas now ship with full self-driving hardware—a major strategic disclosure; R42 discloses that leased Model 3s will not be purchasable because Tesla plans a ride-hailing network. R34 restates a 2015 net-zero commitment already achieved; R41 lists 20 destinations in an already-announced programme. The dense model rewards genuine novelty disclosure.

proposals.name: Concision and Information Density
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release delivers substantial, substantive information in a compact format with minimal repetition, throat-clearing, or self-congratulatory padding. Score 0 if the release is lengthy relative to its news content, with extensive repetition, background filler, or decorative language.
proposals.rationale: R07/R33/R59 deliver national economic data in under 200 words each; R01 makes a complete data-backed rebuttal in one page. R51 is a long, padded piece about office reopening filled with diagrams and clichés ('light dimmer, not a light switch'); R49 is a lengthy CSR letter with minimal specific content. The dense model appears to reward information-per-word.

proposals.name: Named Individuals Performing Specific Actions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the release names specific individuals and describes concrete, distinctive actions they personally took (not merely their title or a generic quote). Score 0 if all people mentioned are identified only by title and contribute only generic statements.
proposals.rationale: R05 identifies RGJ employees whose Jeep had RGJ decals, describes the driver reversing into a Tesla employee, and names the arresting agency; R06/R44 describes Jerome Guillen creating an entire General Assembly line 'in a matter of weeks' and Kevin Kassekert turning 'a pile of rocks in the Sierra Nevada mountains into a factory employing 12 thousand people.' R43 names employees but only in anodyne testimonial quotes ('Knowing Target provides backup care gives our family such peace of mind'). Named human agency drives news interest.

proposals.name: Standard newswire dateline and formatting
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text begins with a standard newswire dateline (e.g., CITY, State, Month Day, Year / PRNewswire) and uses typical press release formatting markers. Do not judge the quality of the release.
proposals.rationale: Standard wire formatting may correlate with perceived newsworthiness due to distribution tier, but it is a structural artifact of agency drafting rather than genuine editorial value, as seen in R25 and R46.
proposals.upstream_parent: distribution via a major paid newswire or external PR agency

proposals.name: Journalistic article artifacts and bylines
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text reads like a published news article rather than a first-party release, containing elements such as reporter bylines, photograph credits, or third-party analyst quotes. Do not judge the quality of the writing.
proposals.rationale: The presence of journalistic artifacts like photo credits or external reporting framing (R09, R54) signals third-party authorship, which a model might mistake for inherent newsworthiness instead of a distinct source.
proposals.upstream_parent: authored by an external news outlet rather than the organization

proposals.name: Periodic update and templated temporal markers
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text uses standardized temporal and templated language indicating a routine, recurring release (e.g., 'latest results for', 'previous month', 'compared to prior year'). Do not judge the quality or importance of the data.
proposals.rationale: Routine index updates (R04, R21) rely on templated temporal markers that signal their position in an ongoing series, which might inflate perceived importance without reflecting standalone newsworthiness.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in a stream of routine periodic releases

proposals.name: Scraped web page and CMS navigation artifacts
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text contains non-narrative web elements such as sign-up prompts, raw HTML, or literal webpage extraction errors. Do not judge the quality of the content.
proposals.rationale: The presence of raw page artifacts or HTML extraction errors (R50, R16) is a byproduct of the scraping process rather than the text's actual newsworthy value, which can heavily bias text-only models.
proposals.upstream_parent: web scraping or CMS export process

proposals.name: Presupposition of prior event knowledge
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text explicitly references or presupposes the reader's knowledge of a previous announcement or ongoing incident (e.g., 'As you have likely heard', 'The temporary ban has proved effective'). Do not judge the clarity of the text.
proposals.rationale: Language that assumes prior knowledge (R14, R41) reveals that a release is a later installment in an ongoing event, a temporal position that influences model scoring but isn't an intrinsic quality of the text itself.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in an unfolding event timeline

proposals.name: Colloquial and promotional consumer blog tone
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text uses informal, promotional language directly addressing the consumer (e.g., 'Get excited!', exclamation points, colloquial questions like 'Have you scrambled?'). Do not judge if this tone is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: An informal, consumer-facing tone (R01, R19) reflects the intended distribution channel (a corporate blog) rather than the actual editorial newsworthiness of the announcement.
proposals.upstream_parent: intended for a consumer-facing blog rather than the media

proposals.name: Legal and regulatory compliance phrasing
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text contains strict legal, regulatory, or compliance terminology (e.g., 'confidentially submitted', 'shall not constitute an offer', 'settlement', 'due process'). Do not judge the legal soundness.
proposals.rationale: The use of dense compliance language (R36, R57) is a fingerprint of legal authorship mandated by regulatory processes, which may influence scoring without making the item inherently newsworthy.
proposals.upstream_parent: drafted by legal or regulatory compliance teams

proposals.name: Internal memo or open letter framing
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text is explicitly framed as an internal communication, open letter, or email (e.g., 'The following email was sent', 'Dear Host', 'Dear Target Guest'). Do not judge the effectiveness of the communication.
proposals.rationale: Framing a release as an internal memo or open letter (R15, R27) stems from an upstream decision about target audience rather than the objective newsworthiness of the content.
proposals.upstream_parent: intended for an internal or closed stakeholder audience

proposals.name: Reactive crisis management and defensive stance
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text uses defensive language responding to external allegations, accidents, or public scrutiny (e.g., 'completely false', 'strongly opposes', 'we investigate every single incident'). Do not judge the validity of the defense.
proposals.rationale: A defensive stance against allegations or incidents (R34, R52) indicates a reactive crisis management origin; while such topics can be genuinely newsworthy, the defensive language itself is a structural artifact of the PR strategy.
proposals.upstream_parent: reactive crisis management origin

proposals.name: Repeated and duplicated content blocks
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 to 10 the extent to which the text contains verbatim duplicated paragraphs, repeated key takeaways, or identical boilerplate from previous releases. Do not judge the quality of the duplicated text.
proposals.rationale: The presence of duplicated text blocks or identical statements (R03, R48) often indicates a re-issued or syndicated release, a process artifact that artificially inflates text length without adding newsworthy substance.
proposals.upstream_parent: re-issuance or syndication process
